Recurring Deposit (RD): Meaning, Interest Formula and RD vs SIP

A recurring deposit lets you save a fixed amount every month and earn a fixed rate of interest. It suits people without a lump sum, and this guide covers the working, the tax, and how it compares with an FD and a SIP.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

How an RD works

  • Choose a monthly amount, which can start as low as a few hundred rupees.
  • Choose a period, usually from 6 months to 10 years.
  • The rate is fixed on the day you open it, and stays fixed.
  • The instalment is usually auto-debited from your account.
  • At maturity, you get all your instalments plus interest.

A worked example

₹5,000 a month for 5 years at 7%, compounded quarterly. You pay in ₹3,00,000, and the maturity value is about ₹3,59,664, so the interest is about ₹59,664. Each instalment earns for a different length of time: the first for 60 months, the last for only 1.

Compare a ₹3,00,000 lump sum in a fixed deposit at the same rate for 5 years, which would grow to about ₹4,24,433. The FD earns more, as all of the money is invested for the full time. Exact RD values vary slightly with each bank's method, so try the RD calculator.

Types of RD

  • Regular bank RD: offered by almost every bank.
  • Senior citizen RD: at a slightly higher rate.
  • Post Office RD: a five-year scheme backed by the government, with rates set each quarter.
  • Flexi RD: at some banks, you can vary the monthly amount within limits.

Rules worth knowing

  • Missed instalments can bring a penalty, and several missed instalments can lead the bank to close the RD.
  • Early closure is usually allowed, at a lower interest rate and possibly a penalty.
  • Interest is taxable at your slab rate, each year as it accrues, and TDS can apply.
  • RDs have no special tax benefit, unlike a tax-saving FD.
  • DICGC cover applies up to ₹5 lakh, together with your other deposits in that bank.

RD, FD and SIP compared

BasisRDFDSIP in a mutual fund
PaymentMonthlyOne lump sumMonthly
ReturnFixedFixedMarket-linked, not guaranteed
RiskLowLowDepends on the fund; equity is high
Best forShort goals with a known dateParking a lump sum safelyGoals 5 years or more away
Stopping earlyPenalty is likelyPenalty is likelyCan stop anytime; exit load may apply

When an RD makes sense

An RD suits a goal 1 to 3 years away, such as a holiday, a down payment or next year's fees, where you can't risk a fall in value. For goals many years away, a SIP in an equity fund has historically offered better growth, though with real risk. An RD is also a good way for a student to build the habit of saving.

Exam and interview questions

What is a recurring deposit in simple words?

A savings scheme in which you pay a fixed amount every month for a set period, and receive it back with fixed interest at the end.

Is RD better than SIP?

They do different jobs. An RD gives a fixed, safe return for short-term goals. A SIP in an equity fund has no guaranteed return but suits long-term goals better.

Is RD interest taxable?

Yes. It is taxed at your slab rate, and TDS applies once your total interest from the bank crosses the yearly limit.
